title: Build a Basic Histogram
markdown:
### The Scenario
A teacher wants to see how exam scores are distributed.

### The Task
- Use `plt.hist()` to create a histogram of `scores`.
- Use exactly `5` bins.
- Give the chart the title: `Exam Scores Distribution`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

scores =[55, 60, 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 83, 85, 88, 90, 92]

# Create your histogram below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.patches) == 5, 'We expected a histogram with exactly 5 bins.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Exam Scores Distribution', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Exam Scores Distribution.'

title: Customize Histogram Colors
markdown:
### The Scenario
An HR analyst is reviewing interview scores and wants a histogram with clearer styling.

### The Task
- Use `plt.hist()` to create a histogram of `scores`.
- Use exactly `6` bins.
- Set the bar color to `orange`.
- Set the edge color to `black`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Score`.
- Give the chart the title: `Interview Score Distribution`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

scores =[58, 61, 64, 67, 68, 70, 72, 73, 75, 78, 81, 84, 86, 89, 91, 94]

# Create your customized histogram below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.patches) == 6, 'We expected a histogram with exactly 6 bins.'
patch = ax.patches[0]
assert mcolors.to_rgba(patch.get_facecolor()) == mcolors.to_rgba('orange'), 'Your histogram bars should be orange.'
assert mcolors.to_rgba(patch.get_edgecolor()) == mcolors.to_rgba('black'), 'Your histogram bar edges should be black.'
assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Score', 'Check your x-axis label! It must be exactly Score.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Interview Score Distribution', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Interview Score Distribution.'

title: Compare Two Histograms
markdown:
### The Scenario
A gym wants to compare morning and evening workout durations.

### The Task
- Plot `morning_minutes` and `evening_minutes` on the same histogram.
- Use `5` bins for each histogram.
- Add labels so the legend shows `Morning` and `Evening`.
- Show the legend.
- Give the chart the title: `Workout Duration Comparison`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

morning_minutes =[20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38]
evening_minutes =[25, 27, 29, 31, 34, 36, 39, 42]

# Create your overlapping histograms below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.patches) == 10, 'We expected two histograms with 5 bins each, for a total of 10 bars.'
legend = ax.get_legend()
assert legend is not None, 'We could not find a legend. Did you call plt.legend()?'
labels = {text.get_text() for text in legend.get_texts()}
assert labels == {'Morning', 'Evening'}, 'Your legend labels must be Morning and Evening.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Workout Duration Comparison', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Workout Duration Comparison.'

title: Create a 1x2 Subplot Layout
markdown:
### The Scenario
A small business wants revenue shown beside order distribution in one figure.

### The Task
- Create a `1x2` subplot layout.
- In the first subplot, make a line chart of `months` vs `revenue` and title it `Revenue`.
- In the second subplot, make a histogram of `orders` with `4` bins and title it `Orders`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months =['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr']
revenue =[200, 230, 250, 280]
orders =[18, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30]

# Create your 1x2 subplot figure below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()

title: Stack Two Subplots Vertically
markdown:

An ecommerce analyst wants traffic and purchase values in a vertical dashboard.

### The Task
- Set the figure size to `(8, 6)`.
- Create a `2x1` subplot layout.
- In the top subplot, plot `days` vs `visits` and title it `Website Visits`.
- In the bottom subplot, create a histogram of `purchase_values` with `5` bins and title it `Purchase Values`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days =['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri']
visits =[120, 145, 138, 160, 172]
purchase_values =[18, 22, 25, 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 48, 50, 55]

# Create your vertical subplot figure below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
width, height = fig.get_size_inches()

title: Build a 2x2 Visualization Dashboard
markdown:
### The Scenario
A startup wants a quick visual dashboard with four different views of its data.

### The Task
- Create a `2x2` subplot layout.
- In subplot 1, create a line chart of `days` vs `sales` titled `Sales Line`.
- In subplot 2, create a scatter plot of `ad_spend` vs `signups` titled `Ad Spend vs Signups`.
- In subplot 3, create a bar chart of `regions` vs `region_sales` titled `Regional Sales`.
- In subplot 4, create a histogram of `ratings` with `4` bins titled `Ratings Histogram`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu']
sales =[20, 24, 19, 27]
ad_spend =[100, 120, 90, 140]
signups = [5, 7, 4, 8]
regions = ['North', 'South', 'East', 'West']
region_sales =[80, 65, 70, 90]
ratings =[3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 5, 4, 4]

# Create your 2x2 dashboard below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
assert len(fig.axes) == 4, 'We expected exactly four subplots in a 2x2 layout.'
ax1, ax2, ax3, ax4 = fig.axes
assert len(ax1.lines) == 1, 'The first subplot should contain a line chart.'
assert len(ax2.collections) > 0, 'The second subplot should contain a scatter plot.'
assert len(ax3.patches) == 4, 'The third subplot should contain a bar chart with four bars.'
assert len(ax4.patches) == 4, 'The fourth subplot should contain a histogram with 4 bins.'
assert ax1.get_title() == 'Sales Line', 'The first subplot title must be Sales Line.'
assert ax2.get_title() == 'Ad Spend vs Signups', 'The second subplot title must be Ad Spend vs Signups.'
assert ax3.get_title() == 'Regional Sales', 'The third subplot title must be Regional Sales.'
assert ax4.get_title() == 'Ratings Histogram', 'The fourth subplot title must be Ratings Histogram.'

title: Add a Mean Line to a Histogram
markdown:
### The Scenario
A delivery company wants to show delivery times and highlight the average.

### The Task
- Create a histogram of `delivery_times` using `6` bins.
- Add a vertical dashed line at the mean delivery time.
- Give the chart the title: `Delivery Times`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

delivery_times =[22, 24, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 38, 40]

# Create your histogram below



# Display the plot natively
plt.show()
validation_code:
import numpy as np
ax = plt.gca()
expected_mean = np.mean(delivery_times)
assert len(ax.patches) == 6, 'We expected a histogram with exactly 6 bins.'
assert any(np.allclose(line.get_xdata(), [expected_mean, expected_mean]) for line in ax.lines), 'Add a vertical line at the mean using plt.axvline().'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Delivery Times', 'Check your plot title! It must be exactly Delivery Times.'
